Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/Quality enforcement into 4.0.0 amendment (2026-10-31)/The qualification runner accepts a peer in a registered fixture worktree

The qualification runner accepts a peer in a registered fixture worktree

TSK-1102todo

After this merges, the qualification operator can run trials under the per-trial `--codex-hook-trust=bypass` option whose subject opens a.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, the qualification operator can run trials under the per-trial `--codex-hook-trust=bypass` option whose subject opens a Codex review seat in its task worktree, as the method prescribes: the peer reaches ready, receives its delivery and the trial finishes with no validity flag from it; under the default `review` option such a peer is still refused at its hook screen; and the runner still refuses any peer whose working directory fails the stated identity checks at any moment it looks.

Context

The native qualification runner (evals/qualification/runner.py) refuses every peer seat a subject opens outside the fixture repository root: check_peer_state compares the peer's working directory with the fixture path and raises "peers start in the fixture repository" (runner.py:1302-1303 at TSK-1094's reviewed head addf25865). The method puts a review seat in the subject's task worktree (cf-herdr "Naming": the intended worktree cwd identifies the seat; .codeflow/rules/worktrees.md: work happens in .worktrees/<slug>), so a subject that follows the method gets peer_launch_refused and its trial is invalid. Evidence: TSK-1032 trial round 7 (.worktrees/tsk-1032/target/qualification/typed-code-r7/builder-adds-type-checker-and-config-model-7/peers.json): the Codex start requested for <repository>/.worktrees/tsk-031 was refused with that message, and observation.json carries peer_launch_refused; round 5 shows the same for .worktrees/tsk-032. Both trials ran under the default --codex-hook-trust=review option (launch.json, hook_trust.option). The sibling tasks TSK-1030, TSK-1031 and TSK-1033 open peers the same way when their subjects follow the method; only TSK-1032's refusal is demonstrated here.

Two more checks are keyed to the root path. trust_choice (runner.py:306-357) accepts a folder-trust dialog only when it names the fixture path, and observe_peer passes Path(run["repository"]) to handle_startup (runner.py:1529). Codex keys hook trust by the absolute path of .codex/hooks.json (evals/qualification/README.md:101), so a Codex peer in a worktree shows "Hooks need review" even after the operator's pre-launch review of the fixture root, and the runner refuses that screen (runner.py:308-311). The worktree does not exist before launch, so print-hook-review (runner.py:1114) cannot cover it.

The subject runs as the operator's user and can write every file the runner reads, git's worktree metadata included. The checks below are therefore bounded evidence, not proof of ownership: each one is a concrete predicate the runner evaluates at a stated moment, and the record names what polling cannot see.

Admission: the directory and its repository identity

A peer's working directory C is accepted when it is the fixture repository root, as today, or passes every check below, all evaluated on the raw path first and on realpaths second, with lstat so that a symlink is seen rather than followed:

  1. Fixture identity, captured once at launch into launch.json (peers.fixture_identity): the realpath of the repository R and the realpath of its common directory from git -C R rev-parse --git-common-dir, which must be R/.git, a real directory.
  2. Placement: C is lexically R/.worktrees/<name>, one level down; R, R/.worktrees and C are real directories, none a symlink; os.path.realpath(C) == C.
  3. Link file: C/.git is a regular file under a small size cap holding exactly one line gitdir: <A>; A, resolved against C when relative, is a real directory lexically R/.git/worktrees/<id>, one level down, with R/.git, R/.git/worktrees and A real directories and no symlink among them; os.path.realpath(A) == A.
  4. Reciprocal pair: A/gitdir is a regular file whose content, resolved and realpath'd, is exactly C/.git; A/commondir is a regular file whose content, resolved against A and realpath'd, is exactly the fixture's common directory from step 1. A changed commondir, a backlink to another worktree, a symlink or any non-regular file in this chain refuses.
  5. Git's own view, read in a clean subprocess environment (every GIT_* variable unset, GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL=/dev/null, GIT_CONFIG_NOSYSTEM=1, HOME set to an empty temporary directory): git -C R worktree list --porcelain lists a non-main worktree entry whose realpath is C, neither bare nor prunable; git -C C rev-parse --git-common-dir realpath'd equals the fixture's common directory; git -C C rev-parse --show-toplevel realpath'd equals C. A git error, a missing, ambiguous or prunable entry refuses.
  6. The accepted identity is pinned to the launch at bind: C, A, the common directory and the SHA-256 of the contents of C/.git, A/gitdir and A/commondir. A later check that yields a different identity, including a re-registered A, is a failure, never a new acceptance.

Names are never matched. Other worktree locations (.claude/worktrees, harness homes) and nested directories stay refused.

Revalidation: when the checks run

The identity checks, and under --codex-hook-trust=bypass the hook content checks against C/.codex (codex_hook_preflight on the worktree: hooks.json equal to the shipped contract-3 definitions, no other hook source, no symlink; the evaluator-home checks as today; hooks_sha256 is the hash of the file the peer's Codex reads), run at every one of these moments:

  • when a request is answered (peer_decision);
  • at bind (verify_peer_process from observe_peer);
  • inside before_key, immediately before every startup key (accept_workspace_trust, decline_renderer), in addition to the process identity recheck it makes today;
  • at readiness, before the ready record is written;
  • on every later poll of a launch whose status is ready: observe_peer no longer returns before verification for a ready launch (runner.py:1514).

A failure at any moment revokes the ready record (set_gate(run, pane, None)), sets the launch to unverified with the failing predicate in error, and the trial carries peer_launch_unverified; no key is sent and nothing restores the launch. identity_of (runner.py:1419) stays the process identity; the pinned worktree identity is checked beside it, not folded into it, so a registration-only change with pid, argv, cwd and environment unchanged is still caught.

Limitation, stated in the README: the watcher polls, and a gap longer than WATCH_GAP_SECONDS between two completed polls invalidates coverage (peer_watch_incomplete, read back by watch_gaps); the watcher does not guarantee a poll within that interval, cannot see a change removed and restored between two polls, and no check-then-use step is atomic against an unrestricted same-user writer. This is the runner's existing posture for root peers; the new paths add no stronger claim.

Exact-path trust and the folder-trust finish allowance

The accepted directory becomes that launch's subject path. handle_startup and trust_choice receive the launch's verified cwd instead of the fixture root, so a folder-trust dialog (Claude "Accessing workspace:", Codex "Folder access", Grok "Do you trust the contents of this directory?") must name exactly that path; a dialog naming the root for a worktree peer, or a worktree for a root peer, refuses with no key, as any other path does today.

The folder-trust change finish allows (config_drift, runner.py:1075-1089; codex_trust_entry, runner.py:1026-1038) extends to a trust_level = "trusted" project entry for an accepted worktree path after a recorded folder-trust acceptance for exactly that path. Each recorded acceptance allows at most its own entry, with no other key in it; two accepted worktrees, or the root and a worktree, are each matched to their own acceptance; the rest of the file keeps its baseline (the whole projects table is not stripped); any other folder-trust change stays evaluator_config_drift. This rule covers folder trust only; no hook-trust change is allowed at finish.

The decision and launch records carry the accepted path, its kind (repository or worktree) and the pinned identity, and the refusal text names both accepted forms.

Hook review in a worktree created during the trial: decided, route B

Under the default review option a Codex peer in a worktree meets "Hooks need review" because Codex keys hook trust by the absolute path of hooks.json; the worktree does not exist before launch, so the pre-launch review cannot cover it; and the runner never answers that screen or waits for an answer it cannot attribute to a human (runner.py:308-311). The admission work above does not change that, so under review a worktree Codex peer moves from peer_launch_refused to peer_startup_refused and the trial stays invalid.

Operator decision, 2026-10-31 12:52, saved on the status page and relayed by the coordinator: route B. TSK-1032's trials run with the runner's existing per-trial --codex-hook-trust=bypass, the choice the README already assigns to the person running the evaluation (evals/qualification/README.md:105). Under it the runner's hook content check runs against the worktree's own hooks.json at every moment listed above, and under review a worktree Codex peer stays refused at its hook screen with no key. The runner's never-answer-hook-screens contract is unchanged, and the finish allowance stays folder trust only. TSK-1032's prerequisite: its AC-4 native trials are launched with --codex-hook-trust=bypass once this task lands.

Not chosen, recorded for later tracking if wanted: route A, an operator-authorized, digest-bound review of the shipped hooks for a worktree created mid-trial, which would change the never-answer contract and would first need Codex's supported native trust mechanism investigated. No record owns it; it can be filed as its own task if the default option is ever required for worktree peers.

Alternatives rejected on evidence: pre-creating the review worktree at launch changes a trial that asks the subject to create its own worktree, so its fidelity, although a pre-created path could be verified structurally; waiting at "Hooks need review" in the peer pane cannot tell the operator from the subject typing through the real Herdr binary, and the hook-trust record Codex would write is config drift.

Non-goals: Herdr's own worktree create|open stays refused in peer_shim.py; the subject seat's checks, the peer flag allowlist, the plugin checks and every other refusal are unchanged; the runner never answers a hook screen; no hook-review bypass is added beyond the existing per-trial option.

Context

Context

Two harness sandboxes stop a builder before its first commit. Codex builder seats (the cf-builder posture) cannot finish a build here: the Codex sandbox denies the .git/config write git worktree add makes, denies ps, which coordination/scripts/gate-turn.sh uses to prove a ticket holder is alive, and denies the gate lock holder record under ~/.codeflow/locks/ (full-gate.lock: Operation not permitted), so a Codex builder cannot claim, run codeflow reserve or push (queue items 29 and 29b, 2026-10-31; TSK-1077, TSK-323 and TSK-330 were reassigned to Claude builders for this reason). In a scaffolded project, Claude's sandbox write-deny on .claude/ (an enforcement path) makes the required git worktree add fail on .claude/agents/*.md, so a subject cannot start a task worktree without the auto-mode unsandboxed retry; in the TSK-1032 trials one subject stopped to ask the user and the other retried with the sandbox off (queue item 30, 2026-10-31 01:15). Every Claude builder and every adopter on the sandboxed preset meets this.

This task gives both a sanctioned route that works inside the sandbox without weakening any deny: codeflow work claim (one step with the claim commit and preflight, operator decision D4 of 2026-11-01) creates the worktree through a route the presets allow, with the enforcement-path denies judged on the worktree's own copies after checkout as TSK-399 requires; the Codex builder posture gets a lock home its profile allows and a liveness proof that does not need ps. Non-goals: no deny is relaxed, no preset gains a broad allow, and the coordination scripts are the workspace's (coordination/ is not in this repository); this task changes the shipped posture and the codeflow commands they call.

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/Quality enforcement into 4.0.0 amendment (2026-10-31)/Seat trust prompts follow a recorded hook-trust rule, else the operator

Seat trust prompts follow a recorded hook-trust rule, else the operator

TSK-1108todo

After this merges, an agent running a Herdr seat in any project knows from the shipped instructions that a hook-trust prompt goes to the.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, an agent running a Herdr seat in any project knows from the shipped instructions that a hook-trust prompt goes to the operator unless that project records an operator-authorized hook-trust rule, how it verifies the rule is landed, current and unrevoked, what the rule lets it approve and how it checks the hooks, and what it must refuse; in this repository the recorded rule lets it answer the prompt itself.

Context

On 2026-10-30 at 20:00 the operator gave a standing rule directly in the coordinator's session (queue item 28): in this repository, agents answer Herdr seat hook-trust and folder-trust prompts themselves after reading each prompt in full, and approve once only CodeFlow's own hooks that match origin/main, never trust-all unread and never always-approve. On 2026-10-31 at about 17:15 EDT the operator confirmed it directly in the coordinator's session: "yes, agents should be able to answer the herdr prompts on the sessions that they manage including folder trust and hook trust prompts - or else we can't have autonomy - the key is to have things protected in other ways including sandbox and the guards and other protections." The scope is the Herdr seats the agents manage in this repository's worktrees, folder trust and hook trust. That rule is this repository's recorded hook-trust rule, and its home is one line in the project section of this repository's AGENTS.md (the AGENTS.md row "receive a standing operator rule"; cf-method/references/autonomy.md "Recorded rules and delegations"; no config key holds seat prompts).

It is not a default for adopters. The shipped texts say hook trust is the operator's: cf-herdr/SKILL.md:128 and :181, transport.md "First-run prompts" (ADR-0075, amendment of 2026-10-03), and autonomy.md "Trust prompts" (near :133) and its hook example (near :230), which say an agent never answers a hook-trust prompt. An adopter whose operator gave no such rule keeps that route. This task makes the shipped rule conditional: a hook-trust prompt goes to the operator unless the consuming project's own AGENTS.md project section records an operator-authorized hook-trust rule that meets the landed-record checks of "Recorded rules and delegations" (present on the protected target branch as fetched from the canonical repository, landed by a pull request a person merged, citing the operator's approval as the forge attributes it, with the actions, the trusted ref and the revocation event named). Under such a rule the agent approves once, after reading the whole prompt, only when every hook file the prompt names is byte-identical to the trusted ref's copy, and refuses and reports everything else. The folder-trust text matches the workspace rule of 2026-09-22 already in autonomy.md "Trust prompts".

The same shipped section today rules this out: autonomy.md:160 says a delegation names a human delegate, and :205-209 say delegation never transfers hook trust and a person performs it, and ADR-0075 (its 2026-10-03 amendment, and "Hook trust is the operator's" near :327) says agents never review or trust hook definitions. This task therefore reconciles that section and the ADR explicitly rather than adding a sentence that competes with them: the hook-trust rule is a narrow standing rule the operator authorizes for one project, not a delegation to a human delegate; the human-delegate rule stays for every other delegated decision; the hard gates stay (canonical repository, protected target, an independently attributable human merge, the operator's approval evidence; a timestamp, a chat message or a peer's claim never satisfies them); credentials, protected branches and irreversible actions stay a person's. Before every answer the seat checks the grant is current and unrevoked: fetch the protected target from the canonical repository, confirm the line is present at the fetched tip and its landing pull request and approval still verify, and confirm no later landed change or ADR-0075 amendment withdrew it; a grant that is missing, unreadable, unlanded, unverifiable or revoked keeps the operator route.

ADR-0075's 2026-10-03 amendment also states the condition under which its decision admits an exception (:482-495, :504-506): identical hook definitions do not mean identical executed code, since an unchanged hook can run a changed repository script or a different codeflow through the seat's PATH, a wrapper, a symlink, an alias or shell initialization; and a prompt can hide an incomplete or bundled inventory (Codex shows a count, "trust all" takes inline, user, global and plugin hooks; Grok project trust also grants MCP and LSP servers). The exception returns only after a qualified procedure establishes the complete trusted inventory and the seat's actual execution identity, proven by a live canary on the harness version in use. This task carries that condition into its positive approval rule: a byte-identical definition is necessary and not sufficient; the seat approves only when the procedure has established, for that harness version, the complete inventory the prompt grants and that the hooks' commands, scripts and the codeflow they resolve in the launched seat are the trusted ones. Amended 2026-10-31 after the operator's confirmation: a harness version with no recorded qualification does not send every prompt back to the operator. The seat runs the comparison and the canary when it can and records the result; on a version not yet qualified the primary decides after reading the prompt and the comparison, with the sandbox, the guards and the deny rules as the protection the operator named. The shipped default for a project with no recorded rule stays the operator route. AC-1 chooses the bounded procedure; no new subsystem is planned.

This changes an authority boundary in shipped instructions and in an ADR, although no hook byte changes, so the one whole-unit review carries the security checklist. Non-goals: no change to the hooks, the guards or what a seat may run; the qualification runner's hook-review decision in TSK-1032 (PR 447) is not settled by this text. TSK-1102 owns the runner's per-trial --codex-hook-trust=bypass route; this task neither changes nor relies on it.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, a reader who sets Size in cf-present sees every line on the page scale, stage content included, and nothing on the page renders under the readable floor.

Context

The operator said on 2026-10-31 11:10 that cf-present and cf-docs-portal pages are hard to read and have no aesthetics, and asked for both to reach the standard of a well-designed website (type, palette, spacing, hierarchy, charts, chips), with the artifact-design guidance as reference and the 4.0.0 status report page as the reference look (queue item 36). The design audit of 2026-10-31 (Source, below) found the first cause: Size is a token multiplier on a fixed 16px root (styles.css:50-58, :113-115, :344). Compact 0.94, Default 1 and Large 1.12 scale only the --cf-fs-* tokens, so every rem or px an author writes in an html stage ignores the setting; the status report's stages stayed at 11.5 to 13px at every Size (10 rules at 0.82rem, 9 at 0.78rem, 7 at 0.72rem, 4 at 12px in export-light.html), and the runtime's own kickers sit at 0.7rem (styles.css:421, :436, :449, :479), under its declared 12.5px floor (:58). document-authoring.md gives authors no type guidance.

This task makes the root the scale: html { font-size } per Size step (Compact 15px, Default 17px, Large 19px), every runtime token in rem, the stage host inheriting the ui size, nothing under the floor, and the type scale the audit sets (display 2.35rem, section 1.65, subsection 1.25, lede 1.18, body 1, ui 0.88, caption 0.82, micro 0.76; labels that name structure leave mono for the body face). The Display panel gains a Headings choice (body face or a bundled display face) and a live preview that shows a figure label and a stage line, so Size is seen to scale them. It is first in the redesign because every later mockup and screenshot depends on it. Non-goal: palette (TSK-1110), frame chrome (TSK-1111), stage at-rules (TSK-1112).

Context

CodeFlow holds its adopters to the rule that tooling is tested code (TSK-1031) and plans an 80 coverage floor for every test-running target (TSK-1006), while its own scripts are not all held to either. TSK-1031's first-pass survey (TSK-1031.md, "First-pass survey") found that .codeflow/test-config.json runs the scripts/test_*.py files with no coverage, that scripts/changelog_split.py, scripts/gate-binary.py and scripts/coverage-shards.py have no test file, and that the Python files shipped under assets/ (the cf-evaluate-model and cf-herdr scripts) are under no coverage target; TSK-1031's non-goals leave this repository's own untested scripts to be recorded and routed, and the operator asked on 2026-10-31 who owns them. This task owns them: every script this repository ships in assets/ or runs from scripts/ has tests in a test-executing target, those targets report coverage per target, and the result counts toward the floor TSK-1006 enforces, so TSK-1006's whole-of-main evaluation (its AC-10) finds the tooling covered or admitted with a fix task rather than unmeasured. Non-goals: the floor's enforcement and exemption semantics (TSK-1006), the instruction text (TSK-1031), the assurance record per shipped executable (TSK-1043, which reads the coverage this task produces).

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/Dashboard shell and reuse amendment (2026-10-31)/cf-present documents open in a dashboard shell with a side menu, tabs and drill-down views

cf-present documents open in a dashboard shell with a side menu, tabs and drill-down views

TSK-1120todo

After this merges, an author of any present document can declare a tree of views and the runtime draws it as a dashboard with a side menu.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, an author of any present document can declare a tree of views and the runtime draws it as a dashboard with a side menu, tabs, a context strip and drill-down with a breadcrumb, under one layout contract and view-kind registry, with a linear document rendering as before.

Context

The operator's feedback of 2026-10-31 on the hand-built 4.0.0 status page: a report page needs proper structure for how it reports different aspects, changed by choosing a tab or the like; a proper side menu, like a proper dashboard, with drill-downs; even tasks need proper context sometimes; and this belongs in cf-present, not only for reports, neither rigid nor random, so that each page is not a fresh design with no consistency. Today a present document is one linear block list: the chrome lists the top-level sections in a fixed rail (crates/codeflow-present/web/src/chrome.tsx:1718, cf-section-route), a tabs block switches peer panels inside one place (crates/codeflow-present/src/document.rs:151; document-authoring.md "Progressive depth"), a disclosure nests detail, and nothing lets a reader move from a release to an epic to a theme to a task and back, or see a task with its own context. The 4.0.0 status page built that shell by hand in an html page outside the runtime (its source codeflow-400-status.html: a sections nav and eleven titled sections), which is the inconsistency the operator named.

Outcome: a schema_version: 2 document may declare views: a tree of titled views the runtime draws in a dashboard shell with a side menu (the view tree, the current view marked, collapsing to a drawer at phone width), a header carrying the document's anchor, a view body of catalog blocks, an optional context strip per view (short labelled facts such as an item's outcome, location, owner, state and window), tabs for peer aspects inside a view, and drill-down links that open a child view with a breadcrumb back; a stable layout contract names these regions and the component set that fills them, with a registry of view kinds that has room for a new kind; a linear document without views renders exactly as today.

Figure: the shell's regions; the side menu is the view tree, the breadcrumb is the path down it, the context strip is the current view's facts, and tabs switch aspects inside the view.

Decisions, each reversible and disclosed here:

  • The shell is declared, not drawn by the author. The document gains an optional views array beside blocks; a view has id, title, kind, optional context (one to eight labelled facts, each label, text and an optional state or location mark from the grammar vocabulary), blocks (the existing catalog; tabs and disclosure included) and children (nested views). The root blocks of a document with views are the header's anchor (the first narrative and the orienting figure, as the bar of TSK-1097 requires) and render above every view. A reference of kind view (document.rs:514, the existing frame-reference shape) in any block opens that view; the runtime draws the breadcrumb from the tree, never from the author. The side menu lists the tree to the depth the document declares, with the current view marked and the view's summary mark or count when it carries one (TSK-1096 AC-9's summary vocabulary); at phone width it is a drawer behind one button. The sections rail of today lists the current view's sections inside the body.
  • Outcomes first is the contract's primary structure. The operator's direction of 2026-10-31 (13:15): a report is organised by outcomes first, and every outcome opens to its detail. The contract therefore fixes the root view as an overview whose body lists the document's outcomes (each with its state, percent and next step where the kind has them), each outcome a view reference into its own topic view, and the tree under a topic going to item views and their evidence; the side menu's first group is those outcomes, and other kinds (list, timeline, issues, decisions, evidence, commands) are cross-cutting entries after it. This is the shape every registry document has, not an option an author picks.
  • View kinds are a registry, with room. kind is one of overview (the first view, the outcomes and the decision picture), topic (a group of items with a percent, what it is, done and not done, and its reasoning), item (one thing with its context strip), list (an encoded table of items), timeline (a schedule figure and its windows), issues (blocked and owed items), decisions (operator inputs as decision and form blocks), evidence (coverage and refs), commands (one runnable script) or custom with a one-line reason. The registry fixes what a reader finds in each kind (the layout contract below) and present check warns on a custom view, naming the registry, so a new kind that recurs is added to the registry with a specimen once, and never improvised. Adding a kind is a change to this registry and its specimen, not to the shell.
  • The layout contract. One reference section in document-authoring.md names the regions (side menu, header, breadcrumb, context strip, tabs, body, drawer), the order a view's body follows (lead line, the answering figure or encoded table, short acting text, then disclosures), the component set that fills a body (the catalog blocks, the figure families, the encoded table, the schedule family, the decision and form blocks, labelled code), and what each registry kind must carry; the specimen page renders every kind once. A document that follows the contract looks like every other document that does, and the contract leaves content free; it is the consistency the operator asked for and the custom kind is the flexibility.
  • Drill-down is navigation, not duplication. A child view is declared once and reached from any reference; the same task view serves the release, the epic and the theme that link to it. The breadcrumb is the declared path to the current view; a reference from elsewhere keeps the tree's path, so a reader always knows where a view lives.
  • Export and comments. The export renders the shell with the side menu as a static outline, every view present in tree order with its breadcrumb as a heading path, and the first view shown when scripts are off, so a capture holds everything. Comment anchors bind to blocks inside views as they bind today; a view id is part of the anchor's context so a moved block in another view is not re-anchored by mistake.
  • Capacity holds the largest report it must carry (Codex round 8, F1). A status document for a scope of 300 tasks declares one item view per task (TSK-1098 AC-10), so a document-wide cap of a few dozen views or 512 blocks (limits.rs:5, MAX_BLOCKS; :11, MAX_FIGURE_BLOCKS 24) cannot hold it. The budgets are therefore scoped: the existing block, nesting and figure budgets of limits.rs apply per view (each view is one block tree of at most 512 blocks and 24 figures, as a linear document is today), and the document gains a view budget of 1024 views, a view depth of four and a total of 16384 blocks and the existing 8 MiB document size, each refused by name; the runtime renders the current view into the page and keeps the other views as parsed data, so a large document stays responsive, and the export writes every view. Every task stays reachable through the outcomes path; the generator never drops a drill-down to fit, and a document over the budget is refused, never truncated.
  • The stored revision is bounded with the document (Codex round 9, F6). The store pretty-serialises each revision (state.rs:4196), update publishes a revision and moves the current-session pointer without checking that revision's own read limit (state.rs:1250, :1259), and every later read enforces MAX_REVISION_STATE_BYTES, the document budget plus 1 MiB (limits.rs:63, state.rs:4020). A 16001-block document of short narratives fits 8 MiB compact and exceeds that read limit once pretty-printed, so it would open, store and then never read, show or export again. This task owns the reconciliation: before open or update writes anything, the store serialises the revision envelope exactly as it will persist it (RevisionContent, context and snapshots included) and refuses by name when that representation would exceed the read limit, before any session state changes, so the current revision never advances to one that cannot be read back; the resource bound stays, and the accepted document budget is whichever is smaller of the declared block and byte budgets and the representation bound. The builder decides in AC-1 whether to keep pretty serialisation with the read limit raised to hold the declared budget plus its formatting overhead, or to store compact JSON under the present limit, and records the choice; either way the pre-write check is what admits a revision. A custom view, title, label, text and reason are text through the existing sanitiser; html stages inside a view keep their frame and sandbox (ADR-0049).
  • Check ownership (Codex round 8, F4). This task owns the present check warning for an html stage in a view whose registry kind names a catalog carrier for its content (a timeline view with a stage instead of the schedule family, a list view with a stage instead of an encoded table); TSK-1121 owns the missing-topic warning; TSK-1097 carries the guidance for both and neither check.

Non-goals: the status report's own views (TSK-1098); topic identity and per-view change marks across revisions (TSK-1121); new block kinds (TSK-1113, PR 449) and the figure frame chrome (TSK-1111, PR 449); the portal (TSK-1114, PR 449), whose pages keep their committed source and route identity under the portal content contract and share only the composition guidance; a page builder or a stored layout.

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/Dashboard shell and reuse amendment (2026-10-31)/A present document on a topic is revised in place with its version history and per-view change marks

A present document on a topic is revised in place with its version history and per-view change marks

TSK-1121todo

After this merges, a session that presents a topic again updates the topic's existing document instead of opening a new one.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, a session that presents a topic again updates the topic's existing document instead of opening a new one, the reader sees which views and blocks changed since the previous revision, and an author or generator carries prior blocks forward unchanged by their ids.

Context

The operator's feedback of 2026-10-31: things must be reused where it makes sense, each time a report on a topic is presented, so tokens and effort are not wasted redoing them, with proper revision or versions; and it cannot be random, with too much change and no consistency from one report to the next. The runtime already keeps immutable revisions per session with a block digest per block (crates/codeflow-present/src/state.rs:137, RevisionRecord; revision.rs:141, diff marks a block unchanged or changed by digest) and codeflow present update <session> <file> --expected-revision N adds a revision (cf-present/SKILL.md section 4). What is missing is the topic: nothing ties a new document to the sessions that presented the same subject before, so a session asked for the same report opens a new session and redraws everything; nothing shows a reader which views changed since the previous revision; and an author who wants to carry a prior revision's blocks forward has no command for it, so the blocks are rewritten and drift.

Outcome: a document may declare a topic (a stable key such as status:epc-022 or design:present-shell; a generator derives it by lower-casing its scope key, so one scope always yields one topic); present list --topic <key> finds its sessions and present open on a document whose topic has an open session says so and offers update; a revision's shell marks each view and each block changed, unchanged, new or removed against the previous revision from the stored digests, in the side menu and on the view, with a "since revision N" line in the header; present show <session> --revision N --blocks <ids> and --view <id> print a prior revision's blocks as document JSON so an author reuses them unchanged; and present diff groups its result by view.

Figure: the second report updates the first report's session; the runtime, not the author, works out what changed, from digests it already stores.

Decisions, each reversible and disclosed here:

  • A topic is a key in the envelope, topic, optional, lower-case words, digits, :, ., _ and -, at most 80 characters; it names a subject, never a revision. The session store indexes sessions by topic under the present state directory; present list --topic lists them newest first with revision count and last update; present open of a document with a topic that has an open session prints the session id and the update command and opens a new session only with --new-session, so reuse is the default and a fresh start is a stated choice. A closed session on the topic is listed and never reopened (SKILL.md section 4).
  • Change marks come from digests, never from the author. On a revision after the first, the renderer compares each block's digest with the previous revision's by block id (block_digest, state.rs, which serialises one block) and each view's digest by view id, where a view's digest covers its title, kind, context strip, the ordered ids of its blocks and children, and its place in the tree (Codex round 8, F2): a view is changed when any of those changed or any block in it changed, was added or removed, unchanged otherwise, new when its id is only in the new revision and removed when only in the old, listed in the header line and shown struck in the menu; a block id present only in the new revision is new, only in the old is removed and listed in the header line. A changed context strip with identical blocks is therefore changed, and a view moved under another parent is changed with "moved" as its word. The marks draw with the grammar vocabulary (two non-hue channels, the word in the accessible tree), on the side menu beside each view and as a small chip on the view's header; the header carries "since revision N: so many changed, new, removed"; the first revision carries no marks. A block whose id changed is new plus removed, which is the cost of breaking the id and is said in the authoring reference, so authors keep ids stable for conceptually unchanged blocks (the rule SKILL.md already states). The marks are a reading aid; they never change comment anchors or the feedback lifecycle.
  • Reuse is a read, not a copy inside the runtime. present show <session> --revision N --blocks <id,...> and --view <id> print the named blocks of that revision as document JSON an author pastes or a generator reads, so a repeat report carries unchanged sections forward byte for byte and only revises what the facts changed; a generator that writes the whole document (TSK-1098) gets the same effect by writing stable ids and stable content, and the marks then show only real change. No runtime-side merge, template or partial update: the document stays one file an author owns, and the revision history is the version history.
  • present diff groups by view when either revision has views: per view, the block changes as today; a linear document diffs as today.
  • Boundaries: topic is text through the existing validation; the topic index is a file under the session store, never in the repository; no network, no write to any record.

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/CI merged completions amendment (2026-10-31)/A completion that reaches a task range unchanged through a merge is not bound at the range head

A completion that reaches a task range unchanged through a merge is not bound at the range head

TSK-1123todo

After this merges, a maintainer whose task branch takes another integration line's tip and then builds on it passes `codeflow ci` without.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, a maintainer whose task branch takes another integration line's tip and then builds on it passes `codeflow ci` without reopening a task that line completed, and a completion the range itself adds, changes or reopens is still bound at the head, with later non-planning commits on it refused as before.

Context

Source: issue #455 (CodeFlow 3.1.1, 48104f48b, by an adopter), read on the line tip 79eec1783 after a diagnosis found no open task that covers it. TSK-1083 binds a landed task's own completion and TSK-1066 judges a sync; neither changes which commit a foreign completion is bound at in a task range.

A task branch can merge in another integration line that carries a completed task X. codeflow ci then binds X's completion at the task range's head and refuses every non-merge, non-planning commit on the head's first-parent chain after the merge that brought X in. Those commits belong to the task under review, not to X, so any line that takes another line and then builds on it gets a work.acceptance_binding block against a task nobody changed. No waiver clears it (a waiver is checked for validity only), no planning amendment clears it, and rebuilding the branch moves the block to another commit. The only route the message offers is to reopen X and complete it again at the new head, which attributes the later unit's work to a task that did not do it.

Sites, read on the line tip (the issue cites 48104f48b lines; the code has moved):

  • crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/acceptance.rs:3857 completions_in_range. For a range that cannot be amended (a task range), origin is head_oid at :3956-3961 for any completion that is new against the anchor, including one that arrives unchanged through a merge. A planning or line range binds at introduced (introduced_at, :3945-3954).
  • acceptance.rs:1594 task_landing walks the first-parent chain from that origin back to the merge that brought the reviewed commit and records the first non-merge commit with a non-planning change (after_merge, :1632-1697). It refuses that commit at :1753 ("only merges, planning records and landed line adoptions may follow it").

The issue's reproduction, in a pnpm/Nx monorepo: line A holds task X (complete, reviewed commit R, landing merge on A); line B's tip is a commit; task Y's branch on B merges A's tip, adds 13 of its own product commits and records. codeflow ci --base <B tip> --head <Y head> --branch task/Y --into integration/B blocks X at Y's first product commit. The same tree rebuilt as one merge with A as second parent blocks X on a record file; with A as first parent it blocks X on A's own later commits; with main merged into B first (ci run with --base at that merge) it blocks X on a main commit.

Design (Fable reviews it before the build): a completion that reaches the range through a merge, with its record unchanged since the merge parent that holds it, belongs to the line it came from. In a task range it binds where it was introduced, as a planning or line range already does, and is judged there:

  • introduced_at (:4228-4259) walks back through the first parent and then the second while the parent holds the same complete record and block, so line A may be either parent of the bringing merge. The shape with A as first parent is in scope; it is refused today because stacked stops when the reviewed commit is not on the first parent (:1519-1522), and a head merge that changes non-planning paths is refused as the completing commit (:1680-1684).
  • The completion is bound at that point by the binding the range already runs (bind_completion_with_amendment, :3969-3987), as its own line binds it. It is never skipped unjudged: a record whose bytes match the bringing parent but whose block would not bind on that parent is still refused (AC-4).
  • Commits after the bringing merge on the task's chain belong to the task under review and are judged against its own record, not X's.

What still binds at the head and is refused as today:

  • a record or acceptance block of X that the merge, or any later commit of the range, changes against the parent that holds X's completion;
  • a completion the range itself adds, changes or reopens.

A squashed shape (one merge whose tree also holds the task branch's own product changes) is not a change to X when X's record is byte for byte the copy on the parent that holds it; the merge's other changes are the task's own work under review, judged by the task's own binding and review, and raise no finding for X. Rejected: skipping a completion whose record equals the second parent's copy, because it accepts bytes without judging them and misses the first-parent shape.

This binds trust: the choice decides which completions a task range accepts without re-binding at its head.

Two completions in one range (the reporter's comment of 2026-10-31, https://github.com/sathyassn/codeflow/issues/455#issuecomment-6550610794). The route the refusal offers, reopening X on Y's branch and completing it again at Y's head, cannot pass when Y also completes in that range. reviewed_span_problem (acceptance.rs:1366; the comment cites :816-821 at 48104f48b) lets only the task's own record change after its reviewed commit (SPC-013 R-60), so X's completion refuses Y's record and Y's refuses X's, in any order or commit split. The reporter's workaround is a second, records-only landing for X whose reviewed commit is Y's completion commit.

Decision on the reporter's fallback (allow any planning path after the reviewed commit, as after a landing merge): rejected as stated, taken in a narrow form, in this task's scope because the route this task's refusal prints must be passable.

  • Threat the broad form opens: a commit after the review could change another task's criteria or body, an epic, a spec or a decision record, and the completion would still bind, so a reviewed verdict would cover planning content no reviewer saw. Other rules judge some of those changes, but the binding would stop naming them.
  • Narrow form: after T's reviewed commit, another task U's record may change only when the change is U's status and Closeout (U's reviewed_part, acceptance.rs:245, is unchanged) and U's completion is itself made in this range and binds by its own rules, its own reviewed commit and review included. Any other change after the reviewed commit (U's criteria or body, a status step with no bound completion, an epic or spec) stays refused.
  • Why the narrow form is safe: nothing reaches a verdict unreviewed. U's status and Closeout are the part R-60 already lets a completion write after its review, and U's own binding judges them; the reviewed content of every record is unchanged.

Non-goals: the sync-merge check (TSK-1066), the landed-task binding (TSK-1083), a waiver that suppresses binding_problem.

Outcome
The 4.0.0 milestone fixes EPC-022

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/CI merged completions amendment (2026-10-31)/A sync that takes a main task's record unchanged is not a change the line makes

A sync that takes a main task's record unchanged is not a change the line makes

TSK-1124todo

After this merges, a maintainer who syncs `main` into an integration line passes `codeflow ci --branch <line>` when `main` reopened and.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, a maintainer who syncs `main` into an integration line passes `codeflow ci --branch <line>` when `main` reopened and recompleted a task the line has never held, and a sync that edits that record by even one byte still blocks.

Context

Source: issue #456 (CodeFlow 3.1.1, by an adopter), read on the line tip 79eec1783 after a diagnosis found no open task that covers it. TSK-1066 makes a clean sync pass and a hand-edited sync block; neither says what ci --branch <line> does with a main task the line has never held and that main reopened.

A sync merges main into an integration line. main holds a task (TSK-739 in the issue) that the line has never held. On main it was completed, reopened with one added criterion, and completed again. The merge carries main's record unchanged: the blob is the same on the merge and on main's tip. codeflow ci --branch <line> --base <line tip> --head <sync merge> blocks it twice with work.acceptance_binding:

  • "refs/remotes/origin/main (commit ...) records a completion of this task, but it is not the target this run is judged against, so its criteria stay as they were; a reopened task keeps its criteria once a completion of it has landed";
  • "a reopened task keeps its criteria as the anchored target has them; change them in the epic's batched amendment, a planning pull request on the target".

The pre-push check on the same push passed: it judges from main's tip, where the record is current. In the issue's table the task is absent at the line tip, complete (after the reopen and an added criterion) at main's tip, and the same blob at the sync merge.

Sites, read on the line tip. Both quoted findings come from the binding of T's completion, bind_completion_with_amendment, under work.acceptance_binding:

  • The first sentence: recovered_completion (acceptance.rs:2124) finds main's earlier completion, because reopened_in_range (lifecycle.rs:2388-2416) sees main's reopen commit in the sync's range. judge_reopened (acceptance.rs:2257, tips at :2308-2342) does not count the default-branch tip as a criteria base, so the landing is Landing::Unjudged (text at landing.rs:128-130), and the refusal at acceptance.rs:2176-2179 is pushed under work.acceptance_binding at acceptance.rs:657. That refusal keeps the earlier criteria.
  • The second sentence: reopen_problems (lifecycle.rs:1190) compares those kept criteria with the recompleted record and returns REOPENED_CRITERIA (acceptance.rs:3679), pushed under work.acceptance_binding at acceptance.rs:658-663.
  • The same text is also raised as work.criteria_frozen by reopened_criteria (acceptance.rs:3656-3666), but only when the line's base, or its history through RecordStore::recovered, holds an older complete record of T (acceptance.rs:3768-3786). A line that never held T gets Ok(None) there and raises nothing. A line that synced main's first completion earlier does hold it, so that shape can raise work.criteria_frozen as well.

Pre-push passes the default-branch tip as --policy-from (ci.rs:108-113, ci.rs:429-447), which makes that tip a judged criteria base, so neither finding fires there; AC-1 confirms this.

Design (Fable reviews it before the build): a record that the head holds byte for byte as the default branch tip holds it is main's own content, whose criteria main already judged. For that record, ci --branch <line> shall take the default-branch tip as its criteria authority, as the pre-push check does. The choice binds to the default-branch commit and to blob equality, never to a name or a flag, and a record that differs from main's tip at the head, by even one byte, is judged as the line's change.

Blob equality changes only the criteria authority for these two acceptance findings. It exempts nothing else: the status steps a sync carries stay judged one by one as TSK-1036 AC-7 requires (no remote-tracking ref or default-branch tip exempts a step), and the record is still bound and checked for its review and landing.

The issue's related report (a completed task's own branch cannot push its completion, work.stable_planning_anchor) is the family of #454 and is not part of this task. TSK-350 AC-13 covers the work.criteria_frozen shape of #454; the refusal to start from a complete record is still uncovered, and the builder names what it needs in Findings for the primary (AC-1).

Non-goals: the sync-merge hand-edit check (TSK-1066), the status steps a sync carries (TSK-1036), the #454 pre-push family.

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/Pin check amendment (2026-10-31)/A work claim pinned to a predecessor accepts a local copy that is behind the pinned remote tip

A work claim pinned to a predecessor accepts a local copy that is behind the pinned remote tip

TSK-1125todo

After this merges, an agent whose clone holds a stale local copy of a predecessor branch can claim a task pinned at that predecessor's.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, an agent whose clone holds a stale local copy of a predecessor branch can claim a task pinned at that predecessor's pushed tip, while a copy that is ahead of the pin or diverged from it is still refused with a message that names the real cause.

Context

Source: issue #459 (CodeFlow 3.1.1, source 48104f48b), read on the line tip b6cf648d3; the issue's line numbers have moved, and no open task covers it.

codeflow work claim <task> --on <TSK-A>@<sha> refuses with "TSK-A predecessor branch has advanced; rebase on its new reviewed head and recheck" when the predecessor's remote-tracking branch is exactly at the pin and a local branch of the same name sits at an earlier commit that the pin contains. The local copy is behind, not ahead, so the message names the wrong cause and its remedy (rebase on a new reviewed head) does not apply. Deleting the local branch clears the refusal.

Sites, read on the line tip, all in crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/work_start.rs:

  • PinBranches::read (:1100) maps each remote-tracking branch to its tracking name with tracking_branch (:1117-1121) and inserts the commit into one tip set per task and branch name (:1124-1129). The local task/X and origin/task/X therefore share a set, and the set does not record which tip came from which side.
  • PinBranches::pin_name (:1188) finds the one branch name whose set holds the pin, then refuses with "predecessor branch has advanced" when that set holds more than one tip (:1196-1201). It does not look at how the other tip relates to the pin.
  • Callers of pin_name or pin_branch (:1260): reviewed_pins_in (:1403), the helpers at :1502 and :1523, work start at :1573 and validate_dependencies (:2505-2506). The claim reaches it through resolve_pins (crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/work.rs:288-297) and reviewed_pins_in.
  • A second consumer holds the same refusal under another message. stacked_pins (:1763) collects, for each code dependency, every visible tip the pushed HEAD contains (tips_of, loop at :1809) and returns "this branch contains several tips" when more than one qualifies (:1812-1828). A claim cut from the pin has the pin and the stale ancestor both contained in HEAD, so it fails here. codeflow ci calls it on a push (crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/ci.rs:700-708, the note and empty list at :1780-1787), and the pre-push push set runs that command (crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/push_set.rs:297-335). On the error the predecessor's commits are judged in the range (classification.rs:454-459). Today's push check fails in this shape (crates/codeflow-cli/tests/work_cli.rs:1854-1859, :2018-2046); a_claim_on_a_reviewed_head_passes_its_own_push_check (:1880) passes only when the pin is honoured.

Design (Fable reviews it before the build): the refusal exists so a pin is never used after its branch moved past it. A copy of the branch that the pin contains has not moved past the pin, so it is not "advanced". pin_name shall accept the pin when every other tip of the same branch name is a strict ancestor of the pin, judged by descendant_of (crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/history.rs:288-293, which returns an error for an overlay, incomplete ancestry or a shallow boundary), so an ancestry that cannot be read refuses (issue 79), never reads as "behind". A tip that is ahead of the pin or diverged from it still refuses; this replaces today's "advanced" message for those two cases with one that names the branch, both tips (the pin and the other tip), the relation and the fix. stacked_pins applies the same rule: extra contained tips that are strict ancestors of the one tip the claim would accept collapse to that tip, an ancestry error still returns the error, and an ahead or diverged extra tip still returns an error, so the push nomination honours the pin exactly when the claim does. Both share one helper, so the two surfaces cannot drift. The choice binds to commit ids and ancestry, never to a branch name, a remote name or which side a tip came from. pin_name is shared with the pre-push and CI pin checks, so the builder confirms in its findings that no consumer relies on the old refusal for a behind copy, and the review carries the cf-security-reviewer checklist.

Non-goals: adopting an agent's own branch as the claim (TSK-1093), the pin-chain and clean re-merge rules (TSK-341), and the choice between a stale pin and a moved branch for a pin that is not the tip of any copy, which keeps its current refusal.

Outcome

The shipped report specimens and portal layer samples conform to the approved shell and topic contracts

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, the operator and any adopter can open one index of the ten report specimens and three portal layer samples, authored on the approved contracts, each rendered in every theme and mode at desktop and phone width, and see the shipped samples conforming to the approved shell, topic and portal contracts.

Context

The operator asked on 2026-10-31 (the coordinator's handoff, section 5, 18:5x) for proper samples to review of the status report and its variants, of cf-present and of the docs portal, and samples of everything: one present specimen per report type, all ten (status report, epic close, security review, weekly workspace digest, design review, feature, hand-off, incident, research or decision, small project), and one sample page per portal layer (overview, area, reference). The set was first planned in TSK-1097 (AC-19) on the surface that existed then, to be revised here once the shell, topic and portal frame landed, which meant writing every file twice. On 2026-11-01 the operator approved moving the whole set here, so the thirteen files are authored once, on the approved contracts, and TSK-1097 no longer waits for them. TSK-1097's AC-19 now points to this record.

The bar's item (j) binds a recurring kind to TSK-1120's layout contract and view-kind registry and to TSK-1121's topic and stable ids, and the portal samples to TSK-1114's frame. This task starts after TSK-1097 (the bar, the kit, the token system and the checks), TSK-1121 (the topic contract, with TSK-1120's shell and TSK-1122's approved DESIGN_INTENT behind it) and TSK-1114 have landed. It authors the ten specimens and three pages on those contracts and produces the capture set the operator reviews. It changes no runtime and no skill text; a gap it finds in a contract is a finding for that contract's task.

Figure: the samples are written once, after the contracts they must follow, so nothing is written twice and the path to TSK-1120 no longer carries them.

Decisions, each reversible and disclosed here:

  • Which kinds are recurring: the status report, weekly workspace digest, epic close and design review carry a topic and a registry kind; the security review, feature, hand-off, incident, research or decision and small project reports are linear documents unless the registry of TSK-1120 names a kind for them, in which case they take it. The builder records the final list in AC-1.
  • The ten types are a reversible choice taken from the design reference dashboard-v2 (a session scratchpad of 2026-10-31, not committed; TSK-1122 commits the approved prototype). A type the operator drops is removed from the records in one amendment.
  • Homes: the present specimens under cf-present/resources/specimens/, mirrored across the three skill homes; the portal layer samples under assets/docs-portal/starter/samples/, built by the starter's tests, since a fresh codeflow init --standard project has only the three scaffolded docs pages and the starter is the only home every adopter receives. This repository's portal stays the live example of the layers (TSK-446 AC-10).
  • Each specimen is a real document to the bar, built on realistic facts that say they are a sample in the header, never a stub that only declares a main figure.
  • The captures live with this task, under project-management/design/TSK-1127/captures/, with an index page, so the operator reviews one set at the final state.
  • The operator's review of the index page is the audience, never the acceptance: AC-4's acceptance is the checks, the gate and the other-lineage reviewer's read against the whole bar.

Non-goals: new report types beyond the ten (an amendment); the shell (TSK-1120), the topic (TSK-1121), the portal frame (TSK-1114); the bar and the checks (TSK-1097); the status report the runtime generates from live facts (TSK-1098).

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/Status updates ride with the work amendment (2026-11-01)/A status change rides in a PR that is already landing

A status change rides in a PR that is already landing

TSK-1152todo

After this merges, an agent or maintainer can cancel or supersede a task in the PR that settles the work, and `codeflow ci` accepts it.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, an agent or maintainer can cancel or supersede a task in the PR that settles the work, and `codeflow ci` accepts it; no guidance sends them to a PR opened only to change a status.

Context

Operator direction, 2026-11-01 about 14:22 EST: epic and task status updates are marked along with the work that completes them, and no PR is raised only to mark a record done or cancelled, so time, money and CI minutes are not wasted. A task's completion already rides in its own PR. Three places force a status-only PR today: outside_own_record in crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/acceptance.rs (:3249) refuses any change to another task's record in a task PR; task_record_additions in crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/ci/classification.rs (:1020) lets a task PR add only its own record; and the cancellation route for an unlanded standalone task goes through its own plan/ PR (amendment.rs:337, classification.rs:703, project-organization.md:335-344, docs/troubleshooting.md:174).

The change: a task PR may carry the todo or blocked to cancelled change of another task, and the cancelled record of an abandoned standalone task, when the carrying task's own reviewed record names it. The epic close PR carries the epic's complete status with its outcome record; an epic cancellation, a supersession and a follow-up status change ride in an open planning PR or the task PR that settles them. The skills, docs, templates and managed rules say so, and the plan/ cancellation code path stays accepted for records already filed that way but is no longer recommended; with no carrier landing, the cancellation waits on the abandoned branch for the next PR that touches that work. Research and the full place list (25 rows): coordination/coordinators/planning/status-rides.md in the agentic-systems workspace.

Non-goals: no change to the transition table or to completion binding; a task PR still never completes another task or any epic. TSK-1036 AC-4 refuses a head "that changes another record's status"; this task narrows that refusal for the named, status-only cancellation and no other case, and its builder updates the TSK-1036 test fixtures that assert the broader refusal.

Outcome
The 4.0.0 milestone fixes EPC-022

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/Landing candidate admission amendment (2026-11-01)/A landing candidate accepts a task's own criteria change that its pull request already judged

A landing candidate accepts a task's own criteria change that its pull request already judged

TSK-1154todo

After this merges, a maintainer can land a reviewed task whose own criteria changed in its PR through a landing candidate that `codeflow ci`.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, a maintainer can land a reviewed task whose own criteria changed in its PR through a landing candidate that `codeflow ci` accepts, with no separate amendment branch.

Context

Source: issue #488 (CodeFlow 3.1.1, by an adopter), read at commit 4880597073 (the step 4 planning branch head) after a search found no open task that covers it. cf-plan says a task's own criteria change rides in its own PR. A task that rewrites one of its own criteria on its task branch, gets that reviewed and lands it on its integration line still fails codeflow ci on the landing range with work.criteria_frozen. The only way through is a separate records-only epic amendment that copies the criterion byte for byte onto the line first. The adopter paid that cost twice in one day (an extra branch, review, push and CI run each time).

Why no open task covers it:

  • TSK-350 AC-6 (issue #380) gives the task's own PR range, judged with --into <line> and in pre-push, a bounded exception for the task's own criteria change. Its range is the task branch's. A landing candidate is a different range: base is the line tip, head is the tip plus a no-ff merge of the task head, on a branch that is neither the task's nor an integration/ head. Criteria classification gives such a head no own-task identity: with no class it takes the integration/ or amendment path, and otherwise Criteria::Frozen (crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/ci/acceptance.rs:290-345, with task_criteria at crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/acceptance.rs:4394). TSK-350 AC-1 resolves the task from the judged head, but only for a task branch name. This task is the landing half of the same outcome, so it depends on TSK-350 and reuses its rule rather than writing a second one.
  • TSK-1129 (PR 478) lets a task's completion waive a criterion by naming an amendment in its own range; it does not change which range may change a criterion. TSK-1124 and TSK-1152 change work.acceptance_binding for a main sync and work.criteria_frozen for a carried cancellation. None admits an own-criteria change in a landing candidate.

Design. A range whose destination is a confirmed integration line (decided from the destination the run is given and the trusted-line binding epic_line_binding, crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/work_start.rs:883, never from the head's branch name) judges each no-ff merge it holds as that task's own range: base is the merge's first parent, head is its second parent. A task's own criteria change brought in by such a merge is accepted exactly when TSK-350 AC-6 accepts the same change in the task's own PR range at that second parent. Everything the merge does beyond that stays judged as today. Fail closed, and bind to base-branch content and exact SHAs. The trusted line tip is the one the destination advertises for that exact ref, resolved once to a commit at the start of the run (the remote-tracking ref as fetched for a local run), never a local branch, a requester-supplied anchor or a commit the head names, as TSK-1089 fixes it (project-management/tasks/TSK-1089.md:60-74). With no --into, as in the issue's invocation, the line is the one fetched integration/EPC-* ref whose tip is exactly the base commit; none found means the range is not a line landing and keeps today's verdict, and two or more refuse. The checked range starts at that pinned tip: a supplied --base that is not the tip does not shorten it, so the whole tip-to-head range is judged, or the run refuses with the cause. The line and the epic come from the trusted records at that tip, the task's declared target is read at the line tip and at the second parent, and a criteria change that no exact parent pair explains is refused. The PR body reason line TSK-350 reads for the task's own PR is not read at landing (a landing candidate has no body to trust); the dated amendment note inside each changed criterion, which cf-plan already requires, is the record that travels with the content.

Decision owner: the operator approved TSK-350 AC-6 (the criteria-authority exception with its binding) on 2026-10-28, and that approval is now recorded in TSK-350's record. This task applies that approved check at the task's own merge in the line landing and moves no other criteria boundary. If AC-1's findings show the landing range needs a different authority than AC-6's, the change goes back as a planning amendment first.

Non-goals: no change to the TSK-350 PR-range verdicts; no acceptance of another task's criteria change; no change to the reopen freeze or to the completion binding.

Outcome
The 4.0.0 milestone fixes EPC-022

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/Landing candidate admission amendment (2026-11-01)/codeflow ci refuses a direct commit on an integration line before the gate runs

codeflow ci refuses a direct commit on an integration line before the gate runs

TSK-1155complete

After this merges, a maintainer sees a direct commit on a landing candidate in `codeflow ci` before the full gate runs.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, a maintainer sees a direct commit on a landing candidate in `codeflow ci` before the full gate runs, so the candidate is rebuilt without a wasted gate.

Context

Source: issue #489 (CodeFlow 3.1.1, by an adopter), read at commit 4880597073 (the step 4 planning branch head) after a search found no open task that covers it. A landing candidate for an integration line held one commit made directly on it (a task's completion record) after a no-ff task merge. codeflow ci --base <line tip> --head <candidate> and the full gate passed; the pre-push hook then refused the push with work.epic_line. The gate (about 12 minutes there) had run on a candidate that could never land, and the candidate and the next two queued landings were rebuilt.

Cause, read on the tip above:

  • The rule is raised only by the pre-push hook: epic_line_push (crates/codeflow-core/src/hooks/git_hook.rs:1302) calls line_adoption::check_range over the pushed range and emits work.epic_line (:1396). Nothing in codeflow ci emits that rule id.
  • codeflow ci runs check_epic_line_with_adoptions only when the head's branch name starts with integration/ (crates/codeflow-cli/src/cmd/ci/classification.rs:639), and that judges the line's range into the default target. A candidate named otherwise, with the line tip as base, reaches no epic-line check.
  • The hook's own doc comment says a range it cannot read is a note because "CI stays the hard line (charter D19)" (git_hook.rs:1293-1301). CI does not hold that line for this rule today, so the hook is the only check.

Overlap checked, none found: TSK-1151 (records-only landing candidates, PR 486, coord/parallel) changes which checks a candidate's class selects (classification.rs), not the epic-line rule; TSK-1089 keys line treatment on a branch's commits for a line-to-main range, not a range onto the line; TSK-433 and TSK-248 are complete; TSK-402 judges a carry merge onto another line and must keep passing here (a merge is not a direct commit). The nearest region is coord/parallel's: this task lands in codeflow ci's candidate classification beside TSK-1151, so the two are one writer at a time, and the candidate-checking route is the parallel lane's to use.

Design. codeflow ci judges a range whose destination is a confirmed integration line with the same line_adoption::check_range the hook runs, and reports the same work.epic_line finding with the same remedy. The destination comes from the run's inputs, never from the head's branch name:

  • With --into <line> (or the pre-push destination), the line is that ref.
  • With no --into, as in the issue's invocation, the line is the one integration/EPC-* remote-tracking ref (as fetched) whose tip is exactly the base commit. Zero such refs means the range is not a landing on a line: ordinary behaviour, with a note that no line destination was found. Two or more refuse, naming them.
  • The line is bound by epic_line_binding (crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/work_start.rs:883) read at the trusted tip, never at the head, as TSK-1089 does (project-management/tasks/TSK-1089.md:60-74). The trusted tip is the one the destination advertises for that exact ref, resolved once to a commit at the start of the run (the remote-tracking ref as fetched for a local run), never a local branch, a requester-supplied anchor or a commit the head names. A line whose authority cannot be established refuses.
  • The checked range starts at that pinned tip, as the hook's range does (git_hook.rs:1361-1369). A supplied --base that is not the tip does not shorten it: the whole tip-to-head range is judged, or the run refuses with the cause. check_range excludes history through the base it is given (line_adoption.rs:185), so without this a base placed after a direct commit would hide it.

A destination confirmed to be something else, such as main, keeps ordinary behaviour: this rule adds nothing there. Fail closed for an intended line: a binding that cannot be established, an ambiguous destination, history that cannot be read, and malformed adoption entries each refuse in codeflow ci with the cause, since CI is the hard line. The adoption entries are the ones check_range already reads (landed at the target or in the line's history); the head alone cannot adopt its own direct commit.

Non-goals: the hook keeps its note for an unreadable range (charter D19); no change to which direct commits an adoption entry may excuse.

Outcome
The 4.0.0 milestone fixes EPC-022

Release/The 4.0.0 milestone fixes/Moved criterion close amendment (2026-11-01)/An epic closes a criterion that moved to another epic, with a waiver naming the moving amendment

An epic closes a criterion that moved to another epic, with a waiver naming the moving amendment

TSK-1158todo

After this merges, a maintainer can close an epic whose criterion moved to another epic with the serving tasks.

The whole outcome and context, from the record

Outcome

After this merges, a maintainer can close an epic whose criterion moved to another epic with the serving tasks, using a waiver that names the moving planning commit, without deleting the criterion line.

Context

Source: issue #492 (CodeFlow 3.1.1, by an adopter), read on the step 4 planning branch head e0494dcb9 after a search found no open task that covers it. A planning-only amendment moves a criterion from epic A (AC-5) to epic B (as its AC-1) together with the tasks that serve it. The moved tasks keep their (serves A AC-5) tags, because their criteria are frozen in the line's range (issue #488, TSK-1154). codeflow epic status A complete then refuses AC-5 as unverified, although A's acceptance block waives it and names the planning-only commit that made the move. The adopter's workaround is to delete the criterion line from A, which leaves the moved tasks tagged with a criterion that no longer exists and which nothing reports.

Cause: serving_tasks (crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/lifecycle.rs:1472-1482) matches a task to a criterion by its (serves ...) tag alone and ignores the task's epic_id. A's AC-5 therefore still has serving tasks, so it is not treated as an unserved criterion (epic_own_block, lifecycle.rs:1548-1560) and the epic's waiver, which epic_waiver_problem (crates/codeflow-core/src/workgraph/acceptance.rs:1126) already binds to a planning-only amendment of that criterion, is never consulted.

Why no open task covers it:

  • TSK-1129 (PR 478 head d1ba70489, TSK-1129.md Description and AC-2 to AC-4) changes the task waiver's own-range route and the planning-only path test that the epic waiver also uses (AC-3). It does not change which tasks count as serving an epic criterion, so issue #492 fails the same way after it. Nothing is added there; this task relies on that planning-only test as it stands and does not change it.
  • TSK-1154 (issue #488) lets a task's own criteria change land. The moved tasks' tags are not a task's own change, and the freeze is not the cause here. TSK-350 is the PR-range rule, TSK-1124 and TSK-1152 change work.acceptance_binding and work.criteria_frozen for a main sync and a carried cancellation. None touches the epic completion check.

Design. A task serves the epic criterion its tag names only while the task's epic_id is that epic. A tag that names epic A on a task whose epic_id is another epic B is a moved serving task and is handled by a recorded move, not by the tag alone:

  • A's criterion carries a recorded move to B's criterion (the form is the dated note that criteria already use, settled in AC-1 against the existing criteria text rules; the existing Moved YYYY-MM-DD sub-bullet is a text-correction note, record_text.rs:40-43 and :64, so the move form must not reuse that word). The move counts only when, read at the reviewed commit, B exists and its status is open (EPIC_OPEN, lifecycle.rs:1034; a complete, cancelled or archived B never counts), the single planning commit that records the move also introduces B's target criterion with the same obligation text and the same (journey) and (after release) tags, and the moved task's epic_id is B. A forged, dangling, self-referencing or pre-existing-destination move grants nothing, so a note cannot aim finished tasks at a criterion B already had.
  • For A, the moved criterion is closed only by a waived row in A's own block that epic_waiver_problem accepts (a planning-only amendment the reviewed commit contains and which amends this criterion) and whose commit is the one that records the move, not an earlier wording change. A verified row, a tick or silence never closes it, and an (after release) source criterion stays on today's deferral path, which a waiver does not close, so moving a task cannot lower the proof a criterion needed.
  • For B, the moved tasks' tags resolve through the recorded move to B's criterion only when those tasks are its only serving tasks, so B's close still needs a complete serving task that verified it, and a (journey) source still needs journey: verified on B. The proof stays with the tasks; only the epic's name changes.
  • codeflow validate --docs warns (does not block) when a task's (serves X AC-n) names a criterion that does not exist, or names an epic other than the task's own that records no move to the task's epic.

Fail closed: a move that cannot be read, or any doubt about it, leaves the criterion served and unverified, as today. Non-goals: no change to the waiver's planning-only test, to the reopen freeze, to task criteria (frozen as the line holds them) or to the criteria-authority rules of TSK-350 and TSK-1154.

Outcome
The 4.0.0 milestone fixes EPC-022
